title: Schema design, normalization, selective denormalization, and data skew
objectives: Design a Salesforce schema by choosing objects, fields, and relationships that match the business grain.
Normalize so each fact lives on one object, then denormalize only when a stamped field is justified and maintained.
Define ownership data skew and parent-child data skew using official 10,000-record guidance.
Refuse dummy parent accounts and dummy owners as a parking lot for unassigned records.
diagnostic_question: Marketing wants 80,000 unassigned contacts under one 'Unassigned' account owned by a dummy user. Before reading, what schema and skew problems do you name, and what alternative would you propose?
definition: Schema design is the choice of objects, fields, and relationships that store business facts. Normalization keeps each fact on one object; selective denormalization copies a value for a stated performance or usability reason. Data skew is a volume concentration that makes sharing maintenance expensive: ownership skew is one user owning more than 10,000 records of an object; parent-child skew is 10,000 or more children under one parent. ([Ownership Data Skew](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm); [Parent-Child Data Skew](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm); [Relationships Among Standard Objects and Fields](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm))
why_it_matters: A tidy-looking dummy account or dummy owner is a common interview fail. Official record-access guidance says those concentrations force huge sharing-table work when a role or implicit share changes. Interviewers also listen for whether you stamp copies of parent fields without a maintenance plan.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a warehouse loading dock. Normalization is one SKU card per product, not rewriting the product name on every box. Selective denormalization is stamping a frequently needed status on the box so pickers do not walk back to the card. Ownership skew is one forklift driver assigned more than 10,000 pallets. Parent-child skew is one pallet stacked with 10,000 or more boxes. Do not park leftover freight on a dummy pallet or dummy driver.
deeper_explanation: Schema design in this handbook means choosing objects (DATA-001), field types (DATA-002), lookup vs master-detail (DATA-003), and junction grain (DATA-004) so each business noun has a home. That object/field/relationship vocabulary is official; the words normalization and denormalization are handbook design language applied to that schema, not a separate Salesforce Setup menu. ([Relationships Among Standard Objects and Fields](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm))

Normalize first: vendor phone lives on Vendor, not copied onto every Property. Denormalize only when you can name the reader (report, list view, mobile) and the writer (formula, Flow, integration) that will keep the copy true. A formula field is often the safer stamp because it is calculated, not a second stored truth (DATA-006).

Ownership data skew: a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object. Common when unused leads or contacts are assigned to a dummy user. Moving that user in the role hierarchy or in a sharing-rule source group forces a long-running recalculation of access rights. Distribute ownership. If skew is unavoidable, official guidance includes placing that user in a separate top-level role and not moving them. ([Ownership Data Skew](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm))

Parent-child data skew: 10,000 or more children associated with a single parent account. Parking unallocated contacts under one dummy account makes implicit-share maintenance expensive: losing access to one child can require scanning the other children. Configure parent-child relationships with no more than 10,000 children to one parent. ([Parent-Child Data Skew](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm); [Takeaway: Tuning Data Relationships](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_takeaway.htm))

Lookup skew (many children pointing at one lookup target) and lock contention during loads are neighboring LDV concerns. Sequence operations by ParentID when loading. Do not invent unofficial lock-timeout numbers. Needs verification of current lookup-skew Help wording before quoting extra numeric gates.

mental_model.analogy: A warehouse loading dock: SKU cards are normalized facts, a stamp on the box is selective denormalization, one driver with 10,000+ pallets is ownership skew, and one pallet with 10,000+ boxes is parent-child skew.
useful_mapping: schema → dock layout of objects, fields, and relationships
normalized field → fact stored once on the SKU card
denormalized field → stamp copied onto the box for pickers
ownership skew → one driver assigned more than 10,000 pallets
parent-child skew → one pallet holding 10,000 or more boxes
dummy owner / dummy account → the leftover pile that looks tidy and performs badly
role move of a skewed owner → restacking the entire dock's access list
where_it_breaks: Salesforce sharing tables are not cardboard pallets; implicit share scans are the real cost.
10,000 is official guidance in Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale, not a hard governor that always errors at 10,001.
A formula stamp is not the same as a stored copy that Flow must update.
The analogy does not encode junction cascade delete or edition limits.

teach_back_prompt: Explain normalization versus a stamped field, then define ownership skew and parent-child skew with the official 10,000 guidance and one dummy-account refusal.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Design the schema from grain: objects, fields, relationships. Normalize first. Denormalize only with a writer. Ownership skew is one user over 10,000 records; parent-child skew is 10,000 or more children on one parent. Never use a dummy owner or dummy account as a parking lot.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I start from nouns and cardinality (DATA-001 to DATA-004). I keep vendor phone on Vendor. If a list view needs a stamp, I prefer a formula or a maintained field. I refuse 80,000 contacts under Unassigned. I cite Designing Record Access: 10,000 for owner and for children, implicit shares, and do not move a skewed owner around the role hierarchy. I do not recite unofficial lock timeouts.

terminology.plain: Choosing objects, fields, and relationships for the business.
terminology.precise: The official Salesforce model is objects, fields, and relationship types. Design means matching grain before adding copies or dummy piles.
terminology.non_example: A spreadsheet imported as one custom object with 80 text columns.

terminology.plain: Store each fact once on the object that owns it.
terminology.precise: Handbook heuristic: vendor phone on Vendor, pairing date on the junction, not copied everywhere.
terminology.non_example: Vendor_Phone__c text copied onto every property.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Formula field: a calculated display, often safer than a stored copy.
terminology.boundary: Not a Setup menu named Normalization.

terminology.plain: Copy a value on purpose, with a writer.
terminology.precise: Handbook heuristic: stamp a field only when a reader needs it and a formula, Flow, or integration keeps it true.
terminology.example: LAB_VendorName__c stamped on a junction for a mobile list, updated by Flow.
terminology.non_example: Copying every vendor field onto Property 'for reports'.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Roll-up summary: official aggregate on a master (DATA-007), not a random stamp.

terminology.plain: One user owns too many records of an object.
terminology.precise: Official: a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object. Dummy-user parking is the common anti-pattern.
terminology.example: All unassigned leads owned by Dummy Integration User.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Queue: a possible owner type; concentrating a queue can still be a volume problem—Needs verification of queue-specific wording.
terminology.boundary: Do not move that user across roles casually.

terminology.plain: One parent has too many children.
terminology.precise: Official: 10,000 or more child records associated with a single parent account; dummy-account parking hurts implicit sharing maintenance.
terminology.non_example: Contacts spread across real business accounts.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Master-detail cascade: delete behavior, not the same as skew.
terminology.boundary: Takeaway: no more than 10,000 children to one parent.

terminology.plain: A parking-lot parent for leftover children.
terminology.example: Account named Unassigned holding all leftover contacts.
terminology.non_example: A real customer account with a few contacts.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Person account: a different model, not a parking lot.

terminology.plain: A parking-lot user who owns leftover records.
terminology.precise: The ownership-skew article's dummy user for unassigned leads.
terminology.example: Integration User owning every imported lead.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Automated process user: still counts as an owner for skew.
terminology.boundary: If unavoidable, isolate the role and do not move it.

terminology.plain: Platform-maintained parent access from child access.
terminology.precise: Parent-child skew is expensive because implicit shares on the parent may require scanning siblings when child access changes.
terminology.example: Access to one contact implying account access that must be rechecked.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: OWD and sharing rules: SEC-004 territory.
terminology.boundary: Do not quote unofficial share-table row counts.

mechanics.after: Written object/field/relationship map plus who will own rows
mechanics.observe: No dummy Unassigned parent or owner in the design

mechanics.after: Each fact on one object; relationships navigate
mechanics.failure: Text copies of parent names everywhere

mechanics.trigger: A list view or integration wants a copy
mechanics.after: Formula or maintained field with an owner
mechanics.failure: A stale text stamp with no owner

mechanics.before: Unknown children per parent / records per owner
mechanics.after: Plan to stay under official 10,000 guidance or distribute

when_to_use: When designing a schema of objects, fields, and relationships and you must decide where each fact lives.
When a request would copy parent fields onto children without a formula or other writer.
When a load or assignment would put more than 10,000 records on one owner (ownership data skew).
When a load would put 10,000 or more children under one parent account (parent-child data skew).
When someone proposes a dummy account or dummy user as a parking lot for unassigned records.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this schema-and-skew lesson as a substitute for choosing lookup vs master-detail (DATA-003) or a junction object (DATA-004).
Do not treat 10,000 as a hard save-error governor; it is official performance guidance.
Do not denormalize to avoid building a relationship or a report type.
Do not use skew talk to replace query-selectivity and indexing (DQM large-data-volume topics).
Do not 'fix' skew by deleting production records from this lesson.
configuration_or_code_location: Object Manager: objects, fields, relationships that form the schema.
Assignment rules, queues, and default owners that can create ownership skew.
Data Loader / Bulk loads sequenced by ParentID per the takeaway.
Role hierarchy placement of any unavoidable skewed owner.

worked_example.scenario: A sandbox marketing lab will import 20,000 LAB_ contacts that are not yet matched to real accounts. A teammate wants Account 'Unassigned' owned by user LAB_Dummy. You must design the schema and assignment without official skew anti-patterns.

decisions.decision: Do not create a single Unassigned account for all contacts.
decisions.because: Parent-child guidance: 10,000 or more children on one parent is skew.

decisions.decision: Do not assign all 20,000 to LAB_Dummy.
decisions.because: Ownership skew is one user over 10,000 records.
decisions.rejected: Dummy integration owner for the whole pile

decisions.decision: Keep account name on Account; use a status field on Contact plus later matching, or multiple holding accounts/owners below the 10,000 guidance.
decisions.because: Normalize the account fact; distribute volume.
decisions.rejected: Contact.AccountName__c text copies plus one dummy parent

configuration_or_code: Create several LAB_ holding accounts or leave Account blank if the model allows, rather than one 20k parent.
Distribute ownership across multiple LAB_ users or a planned assignment rule.
Document that 10,000 is guidance to design against, not a guaranteed error.
worked_example.output: A schema and assignment plan that avoids dummy-pile skew and keeps account identity on Account.
verification: No single LAB_ account has 10,000+ contacts in the rehearsal.
No single LAB_ user owns 10,000+ contacts.
Account name is not duplicated as an unmaintained text field on Contact.
worked_example.self_explanation: I treated dummy piles as a documented anti-pattern, not a convenience.

hands_on_lab.environment: Disposable sandbox; tiny LAB_ volumes that demonstrate the design, not 10,000-row loads.
starting_state_checks: You can create accounts and contacts.
steps: Write a one-page schema: where account name, contact email, and owner live.
Create two LAB_ holding accounts and two LAB_ owners instead of one dummy pile.
Create a few contacts under each; record child counts per account and per owner.
Write why you would refuse a single Unassigned account at 20,000 rows.
guided_completion: If you created Unassigned anyway, delete those LAB_ contacts and split them.
If you added Account_Name__c on Contact, remove it and use the relationship.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Add a justified denormalized LAB_AccountTypeStamp__c only if you also name the Flow or formula that maintains it.
evidence: Written counts per owner and parent.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Delete LAB_ contacts and holding accounts.
Do not load tens of thousands of rows into a shared org.
hands_on_lab.limitations: This lab does not reproduce production sharing-table timing.

decision_table.signal: A fact already lives on the parent object and users can navigate or report via the relationship.
decision_table.choose: Keep the schema normalized; do not copy the field.
decision_table.not: A text stamp on every child 'for convenience'.
decision_table.why: Normalization avoids two truths; formulas can display parent values (DATA-006).

decision_table.signal: A mobile list must show a parent value offline-style and a writer is funded.
decision_table.choose: Selective denormalization with a named formula, Flow, or integration writer.
decision_table.not: Copy the field and hope users keep it updated.
decision_table.why: A stamp without a writer becomes bad data.

decision_table.signal: A load would assign more than 10,000 records to one user.
decision_table.choose: Distribute ownership; avoid a dummy owner. If unavoidable, isolate that user's role and do not move it.
decision_table.why: Official ownership-skew definition and dummy-user warning.

decision_table.signal: A load would place 10,000 or more children under one account.
decision_table.choose: Split parents or leave unmatched children without a dummy account pile.
decision_table.not: Account Unassigned as the parking lot.

decision_table.signal: Someone wants a dummy account so Contact.AccountId can be required.
decision_table.choose: Revisit whether Account should be required, or use multiple holding accounts under the 10,000 guidance.
decision_table.not: One required dummy parent for all leftovers.
decision_table.why: Requiredness is not an excuse for skew.

limitations: Does not measure your org's actual share-table size.
Does not replace Bulk API tuning beyond sequencing by ParentID.
10,000 is guidance, not a documented hard save limit.
security_notes: Skew is a sharing-performance issue, not a reason to open OWD to Public Read/Write without a security review.
A top-level skewed owner inherits access below them—read the ownership article before using that pattern.
Do not use production customer files to rehearse 10,000-row piles.
common_mistakes: Dummy Unassigned account for all leftover contacts.
Dummy owner for all imported leads.
Copying parent names into text fields with no writer.
Treating 10,000 as a hard error code.
Moving a skewed owner between roles to 'clean up' the hierarchy.

troubleshooting.symptom: Sharing or role change runs for a very long time after a dummy owner moved.
check: How many records that user owns.
Whether they sit in a sharing-rule source group.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: The role UI is merely slow.

troubleshooting.symptom: Updates on one popular account lock or run slowly.
check: Child count on that account against the 10,000 guidance.
Whether it is a dummy parking lot.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: The page layout is the cause.

check: Whether phone is stamped on many objects.
Which object is the source of truth.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: A validation rule will fix two stored truths.

production_notes: Rehearse large relationship changes in a recently refreshed full-copy sandbox, as the takeaway states.
Do not move skewed owners in production as an experiment.
No production deployment is authorized by this lesson.

mcqs.prompt: What is ownership data skew in Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale?

options.A: A single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object
options.C: An object has more than two fields
options.D: A report has more than two groupings

mcqs.rationale: Ownership data skew is when a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object.

distractor_explanations.B: Missing role is a different concern.
distractor_explanations.C: Field count is not ownership skew.

mcqs.prompt: What child volume does the parent-child article call out as a common poor-performance configuration?

options.A: A large number of child records (10,000 or more) with a single parent account
options.C: One child with two parents and no junction

mcqs.rationale: Association of 10,000 or more children with a single parent account.

distractor_explanations.B: Two children is not the cited pattern.
distractor_explanations.C: That is a grain error, not the skew definition.

mcqs.prompt: Why is parking leftover contacts under one Unassigned account a problem?

options.A: It creates parent-child skew and expensive implicit-share maintenance
options.D: Unassigned is a reserved API name

mcqs.rationale: The parent-child article uses dummy-account parking as the anti-pattern.

distractor_explanations.D: Unassigned is not a reserved API name in that article.

mcqs.prompt: A dummy user owns all imported leads. What official risk is called out when that user is moved in the hierarchy?

options.A: Salesforce must adjust a very large number of sharing-table entries

mcqs.rationale: Moving a skewed owner in the hierarchy can cause a long-running recalculation of access rights.

distractor_explanations.C: Ownership skew does not convert relationships.

mcqs.prompt: What child-to-parent count does the tuning takeaway recommend?

options.A: No more than 10,000 children to one parent record
options.C: Unlimited children if the parent is dummy
options.D: No more than 2 children on custom objects

mcqs.rationale: Configure parent-child relationships with no more than 10,000 children to one parent.

mcqs.prompt: Vendor phone is copied as text onto every property. What schema issue is that?

options.C: A missing junction object by definition

mcqs.rationale: The fact belongs on Vendor; copies need a writer or should be formulas.

distractor_explanations.B: That is not an owner-count problem.
distractor_explanations.C: A junction may still exist; the stamp is the issue.
distractor_explanations.D: A custom text copy is not a standard field.

mcqs.prompt: When is selective denormalization reasonable in this lesson?

options.A: When a reader needs a stamp and a formula or automation will maintain it
options.B: Whenever a report might one day need the value
options.C: Whenever you want to avoid relationships
options.D: Whenever you have a dummy account

mcqs.rationale: Denormalize only with a named writer; otherwise keep the schema normalized.

distractor_explanations.B: Future maybe is not a writer.

mcqs.prompt: Lookup, master-detail, and junction objects are part of which official schema vocabulary?

options.A: Relationship types among objects and fields

mcqs.rationale: The Object Reference defines those relationship types as how objects associate.

mcqs.prompt: If a skewed owner cannot be avoided, which official idea appears in the ownership article?

options.A: Place them in a separate role at the top of the hierarchy and do not move them out of it
options.B: Give them Modify All Data so sharing does not matter
options.C: Convert all their records to master-detail children of User
options.D: Store owner names in a text field instead of OwnerId

mcqs.rationale: The article recommends a separate top-level role and not moving that user.

distractor_explanations.B: Modify All Data is not the cited mitigation.
distractor_explanations.C: User cannot be used as that MD primary in the usual blocked list.
distractor_explanations.D: Text owner names are not ownership.

mcqs.prompt: Why can losing access to one of 300,000 contacts under one account be expensive?

options.A: Salesforce may need to scan the other contacts before removing parent implicit share

distractor_explanations.D: Queue ownership is a different topic.

mcqs.prompt: The tuning takeaway says to sequence operations on parent and child objects by what?
mcqs.rationale: Sequence operations by ParentID and keep threads on unique record sets.

distractor_explanations.B: CreatedDate is not the cited sequence key.

mcqs.prompt: Is 10,000 a hard save error in this lesson?

options.A: No. It is official performance guidance, not described here as a governor that always errors at 10,001
options.C: Yes. The 10,001st owned record deletes the user
options.D: Yes. It is an edition gate for Professional Edition only

mcqs.rationale: The docs describe probability of performance problems, not a hard insert error in the cited text.

distractor_explanations.B: Do not invent a hard stop.

interview_questions.question: What is data skew in Salesforce schema terms?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A volume concentration that makes sharing maintenance expensive. Ownership skew is one user over 10,000 records of an object. Parent-child skew is 10,000 or more children on one parent.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I cite Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale. I give the dummy-user and dummy-account anti-patterns. I say 10,000 is guidance, not a hard save error. I separate this from query selectivity. I mention implicit shares on parent accounts as the cost of child-access changes.
interview_questions.example: Refusing 80,000 contacts under Unassigned owned by LAB_Dummy.
tradeoffs: Distribute vs isolate a skewed owner
weak_answer_warnings: Saying skew means the org is out of storage

interview_questions.question: Marketing wants all unmatched contacts under Account Unassigned. Your answer?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: No. That is the documented parent-child skew anti-pattern once you approach 10,000 or more children. Split holding accounts, leave Account blank if allowed, or match to real accounts.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I explain implicit-share scans with the 300,000-contact example. I also check who owns those contacts so we do not add ownership skew. I do not create Contact.AccountName__c as a workaround. I offer a matching process and multiple holding buckets under the 10,000 guidance.
interview_questions.example: Design review note rejecting Unassigned as a single parent for 20,000 LAB_ contacts.
tradeoffs: Multiple holding accounts vs blank Account
follow_ups: How would you report unmatched contacts?
weak_answer_warnings: Agreeing because required fields feel tidy

interview_questions.question: When do you denormalize a field on a Salesforce object?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Only when a reader needs a stamped value and you can name the writer—often a formula, sometimes Flow. Otherwise keep the fact on the object that owns it.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I treat normalize/denormalize as design language on official schema. Vendor phone stays on Vendor. If a junction list must show it without spanning, I prefer a formula. Stored copies without owners become two truths. I do not denormalize to avoid a relationship.
interview_questions.example: Rejected Property.VendorPhone__c text; used a formula or the vendor relationship.
follow_ups: Who owns the Flow that updates the stamp?
When is a roll-up the right aggregate?

interview_questions.question: A role change for Integration User has been running for hours. What do you suspect?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Ownership skew: that user owns a huge number of records, so sharing tables are being recalculated. The ownership article warns about moving such users in the hierarchy or sharing-rule groups.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask how many records the user owns and whether they are a sharing-rule source. I do not move them again to 'speed it up.' Going forward I distribute ownership or isolate that role at the top and leave it. I do not invent a timeout number.

tradeoffs: Wait vs cancel a sharing job—Needs verification
follow_ups: Should this user have a role at all?

interview_questions.question: How does schema design relate to lookup, master-detail, and junctions?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Those relationship types are the official schema. Normalization chooses which object holds a fact. Skew checks whether one parent or owner will hold too many rows.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk grain first: one-to-many vs many-to-many. Then I place fields. Then I ask owner and parent counts against the 10,000 guidance. A correct junction can still be skewed if one vendor has 50,000 property pairings. Schema without volume is incomplete.
interview_questions.example: LAB_PropertyVendor__c is correct grain, but one vendor must not collect 20,000 pairings without a plan.

interview_questions.question: An integration will load children. How do you reduce lock and share pain?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Do not target one dummy parent. Keep children per parent under the 10,000 guidance. Sequence operations by ParentID as the takeaway states.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I want unique parent sets per thread. I mention Controlled by Parent where it meets security, because the takeaway says that avoids creating some parent implicit shares. I rehearse in a recently refreshed full-copy sandbox. I do not claim a specific Bulk batch size unless I have current docs.
interview_questions.example: Split LAB_ load files by Property Id instead of one Unassigned parent file.
tradeoffs: One file vs files by ParentID

interview_questions.question: Is 10,000 a platform error you can demo in a 5-row sandbox?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: No. It is official performance guidance. A 5-row lab proves the schema decision, not the sharing-table cost.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I am honest in interviews: I have not timed a 300,000-row implicit-share scan in this lesson. I have read the Designing Record Access articles and I design so we never create the dummy pile. I would use a full-copy sandbox to rehearse real volumes.
interview_questions.example: Lab writes the refusal note instead of inserting 10,001 contacts.

interview_questions.question: How do you explain normalization without sounding like generic SQL class?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I map it to Salesforce objects, fields, and relationships. The vendor's phone is a field on the vendor object. The pairing date is a field on the junction. A text copy on Property is a second truth unless a formula maintains it.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Interviewers want platform nouns. I mention related lists and cross-object formulas as ways to read a fact without storing it twice. I mention skew if copies encourage dummy parents. I do not say labeled drawers or libraries.
